# Data efficiency on HiLiftAeroML {#sec-data-efficiency}

**On the wings, GeoTransolver and Transolver are more accurate than ISLA
on every rung measured at the reporting protocol of 200,000 cells, by 21 to
32% on the 35-case, 4-geometry and fixed-angle rungs, and the sampling
budget does not change that: on the two rungs measured at both budgets the
ratios agree within 0.01 and 0.04 (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA 0.73 at 200,000
cells against 0.72 at 10,000 on the 35-case rung; 0.69 against 0.68 on the
fixed-angle rung).** The ladders below train every architecture on nested
subsets of HiLiftAeroML and on two further ladders that vary what the
training set contains rather than how large it is, and score them all on
the same validation cases with the same instrument. The ordering never
changes. The 210-case, 21-geometry, 510- and 1,260-case rungs are being
measured at the reporting protocol and are pending (@sec-program-status).
What the chapter adds beyond the ordering is *where* ISLA's error comes from on this
dataset: it is paid in distinct geometries rather than cases, it
concentrates in the slat and flap gaps, and it is representational rather
than a data limit. The chapter also carries the one wing result in which
ISLA leads by a factor: trained under a different sampling law, GeoTransolver
and Transolver are 2.4 to 2.6x worse on the 35-case rung and ISLA moves 1%
(@sec-de-training-law). The single-factor ablation at the end prices each of
ISLA's ingredients. Every ISLA number in this chapter's figures and tables
is ISLA unless a collapsed note says otherwise.

Two conventions hold throughout, as everywhere in the book: the metric is
the area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure in float32 (@sec-metrics),
and a ratio between architectures is baseline error divided by ISLA error,
so a value above one would favor ISLA.

```{python}
#| label: setup-de
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
```

## What was measured {#sec-de-setup}

HiLiftAeroML (@sec-datasets) holds 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing
geometries, each simulated at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°. Three
ladders are used here.

- **The case ladder.** Nested random draws of 35, 210, 510 and 1,260
  training cases from a 1,260-case pool, sharing one 180-case validation set
  (@sec-splits). The validation geometries recur in training at other
  angles. The 35-case draw contains 33 distinct geometries and no case at
  18°.
- **The geometry ladder.** 40 cases on 4 geometries and 210 cases on 21
  geometries, each at all ten angles, validated on 180 cases of 18
  geometries that appear in no training set.
- **The fixed-angle split.** 126 geometries at 12°, validated on 18 held-out
  geometries at the same angle.

Every architecture trains under the frozen protocol (@sec-protocol) at the
reporting protocol: 200,000 sampled surface cells per case, 500 epochs,
bfloat16, no augmentation, two seeds, the freestream as a unit direction,
and each architecture at its own best learning rate (ISLA 1e-3, Transolver
3e-3, GeoTransolver the better of 1e-3 and 3e-3, which is 3e-3 on the wings;
@sec-lr-protocol). On the two wing rungs also measured at 10,000 cells the
ratios agree within 0.01 and 0.04 (@tbl-scoreboard-200k-wings). Every
number is a float32 evaluation of the final-epoch checkpoint; no checkpoint
is selected on validation error. Parameters are matched (ISLA 8.9M,
GeoTransolver 9.0M, Transolver 6.0M) and so are tokens per case; the step
cost is in @sec-review-frontier.

ISLA is the shipped configuration (relative frame, @sec-isla; these lanes
carry the total-measure length unit, within 0.4% of the
RMS-pairwise-distance default at the reporting protocol,
@sec-nb-lenrms-200k). At the reporting protocol it is measured on the
35-case, 4-geometry and fixed-angle rungs; the 210-case, 21-geometry, 510-
and 1,260-case rungs are training and pending (@sec-scoreboard-pending,
@sec-program-status).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why every model receives the freestream as a unit direction"}
Fed the physical freestream velocity of 2,679.5 in/s instead, GeoTransolver's
global-context projector collapses to one occupied slice per head and both
baselines lose 3.4 to 3.8x at 35 cases. The mechanism, the control that
established it and the resulting protocol rule are in @sec-part-baseline;
every number in this chapter is a unit-direction number.
:::

## The ladder {#sec-de-result}

**GeoTransolver and Transolver are more accurate than ISLA on every rung
measured at the reporting protocol; the ratios are computed below from the
200,000-cell artifacts, and the rungs without a reporting-protocol
measurement are marked pending.**

```{python}
#| label: fig-hilift-data-efficiency
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The HiLiftAeroML rungs at the reporting protocol (200,000 cells per
#|   case). Surface-pressure error (area-weighted relative L2, float32) for
#|   GeoTransolver (red), Transolver (amber) and ISLA (blue) on the three
#|   rungs measured at this budget: 35 random training cases, validated on
#|   180 cases whose geometries recur in training; 4 training geometries at
#|   all ten angles, validated on 180 cases of 18 never-seen geometries; 126
#|   geometries at a fixed 12°, validated on 18 held-out geometries. Bars
#|   are seed means; dots are the two seeds; the label above each baseline
#|   bar is baseline ÷ ISLA. Panels share no vertical scale, since the
#|   rungs differ several-fold in error. How to read this: GeoTransolver and
#|   Transolver sit below ISLA on every rung. It does not show the 210-case,
#|   21-geometry, 510- and 1,260-case rungs, which are pending at this
#|   budget (@sec-program-status), or the uncertainty from the choice of
#|   training draw, which is three to eleven times the seed spread at 35
#|   cases (@sec-de-controls). Data:
#|   results/p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-19.json (35 cases),
#|   results/p200k_fleet_interim_2026-09-20.json (4 geometries, fixed angle).
#| code-fold: true
F19 = json.load(open(RES / "p200k_fleet_reduction_2026-09-19.json"))["datasets"]
F20 = json.load(open(RES / "p200k_fleet_interim_2026-09-20.json"))["datasets"]
def gt_best(d):
    """GeoTransolver at the better of its 1e-3 and 3e-3 pairs, with the rate label."""
    a = d["arms"]; cands = {k: a[k] for k in ("gt_unit", "gt_unit_lr3e3") if k in a and a[k].get("n_evaluated")}
    k = min(cands, key=lambda k: cands[k]["pressure_l2_mean"])
    return cands[k], ("3e-3" if k.endswith("3e3") or len(cands) == 1 else "1e-3")
def rung(d):
    g, lab = gt_best(d)
    return {"gt": g["pressure_l2_seeds"], "gt_rate": lab, "t": d["arms"]["transolver_unit"]["pressure_l2_seeds"],
            "isla_ref": d["arms"]["isla"]["pressure_l2_seeds"]}
LADDER = {
 "35 cases": rung(F19["highlift_surface_super_scarce"]),
 "210 cases": None,
 "4 geometries": rung(F20["highlift_surface_geometry_super_scarce"]),
 "21 geometries": None,
 "fixed angle": rung(F20["highlift_surface_single_aoa_12"]),
}
PANELS = [("35 random training cases\n(180 validation cases, geometries recur)", "35 cases"),
          ("4 training geometries\n(180 validation cases, never-seen geometries)", "4 geometries"),
          ("fixed angle 12°, 126 geometries\n(18 held-out geometries)", "fixed angle")]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.0, 4.6))
for ax, (title, name) in zip(axs, PANELS):
    r = LADDER[name]
    arms = [("Geo-\nTransolver", r["gt"], "gt"), ("Transolver", r["t"], "t"), ("ISLA", r["isla_ref"], "isla_ref")]
    means = [statistics.mean(v) for _, v, _ in arms]
    for x_, (_, v, k) in enumerate(arms):
        ax.bar(x_, means[x_], width=0.62, zorder=2, **bar_kwargs(k))
        ax.plot([x_] * len(v), v, marker="o", ms=4.5, mfc="white", mec=INK, mew=0.9, ls="none", zorder=4)
        lab = f"{means[x_]:.3f}" + ("" if k == "isla_ref" else f"\n÷ {means[x_] / means[2]:.2f}")
        ax.text(x_, means[x_] * 1.02, lab, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
    ax.set_xticks(range(3)); ax.set_xticklabels([a[0] for a in arms], fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9.5, pad=8); ax.set_ylim(0, max(means) * 1.3); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axs[0].set_ylabel("surface pressure error, area-weighted relative L2 [–]")
fig.suptitle("reporting protocol: 200,000 cells per case; label = baseline ÷ ISLA", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-hilift-ladder

def ratio(a, b):
    return f"{statistics.mean(a) / statistics.mean(b):.2f}"
print("| rung | GeoTransolver (rate) | Transolver (3e-3) | ISLA (1e-3) | GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA | Transolver ÷ ISLA |")
print("|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|")
for name in ("35 cases", "210 cases", "4 geometries", "21 geometries", "fixed angle"):

    print(f"| {name} | {cell(r['gt'])} ({r['gt_rate']}) | {cell(r['t'])} | **{cell(r['isla_ref'])}** | "
          f"{ratio(r['gt'], r['isla_ref'])} | {ratio(r['t'], r['isla_ref'])} |")
print()
print(": The HiLiftAeroML ladders at the reporting protocol (200,000 cells per case) in float32: seed mean (seed range) of surface-pressure error on the shared validation cases, and each baseline's mean divided by ISLA's (below one means the baseline is more accurate). GeoTransolver at the better of its 1e-3 and 3e-3 pairs, the rate named per row; Transolver at 3e-3; ISLA at 1e-3. How to read this: the ordering, not the absolute level, is the result; rows marked pending are training at this budget and join the table as they report (@sec-program-status), and the 510- and 1,260-case rungs have no ISLA arm yet. Same sources as @fig-hilift-data-efficiency. {#tbl-hilift-ladder}")
```

The preregistered bar for an ISLA advantage, baseline ÷ ISLA of at least
1.10 with ISLA lower on two thirds of the cases, is approached on no rung.
At 35 cases and at the fixed angle GeoTransolver and Transolver lead on
velocity and wall shear as well as pressure.

### The same rung under a different training law {#sec-de-training-law}

**On the 35-case rung at the reporting protocol, GeoTransolver and
Transolver trained under the area-proportional sampling law and scored on
the uniform draw are 2.6x and 2.4x worse than their uniform-trained twins;
ISLA is 1% better.** The ladder above holds the sampling law fixed at the
training convention, uniform over cells. Changing it is the half of the
discretization question a practitioner meets when a surrogate trained on one
mesher's output is handed a mesh from another, and it is the one setting on
the wings in which ISLA's lead is a factor rather than a percentage: under
the area-trained checkpoints GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA on the uniform draw is
1.9 and Transolver ÷ ISLA 1.8, against 0.73 and 0.73 for the uniform-trained
pair. The figure, both datasets (the DrivAerML twin at 100,000 cells gives
7.9x, 9.6x and 1.08x) and the mechanism are in @sec-training-law
(@fig-training-law); the scoreboard row is @tbl-scoreboard-training-law.
ISLA's dependence on the training law is weak, not absent: 1% here and 8%
on the cars.

```{python}
#| label: para-de-training-law
#| output: asis
TW = json.load(open(RES / "trainarea_reduction_2026-09-20.json"))
V = TW["verdict"]; A = TW["arms"]
print(f"Trained under the uniform law and scored on the independent uniform draw at 200,000 cells, ISLA reads {A['isla_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.4f}, "
      f"GeoTransolver {A['gt_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.4f} and Transolver {A['transolver_unit_uniform']['mean']['unif']:.4f} (GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA {V['gt_unit_over_isla_uniform_unif']:.2f}, "
      f"Transolver ÷ ISLA {V['transolver_unit_over_isla_uniform_unif']:.2f}, the 35-case row of @tbl-scoreboard-200k-wings). Trained under the area-proportional law and scored on the same draw, "
      f"ISLA reads {A['isla_area']['mean']['unif']:.4f} ({V['isla_area_over_uniform_unif']:.2f}x its uniform-trained twin), GeoTransolver {A['gt_unit_area']['mean']['unif']:.4f} ({V['gt_unit_area_over_uniform_unif']:.1f}x) "
      f"and Transolver {A['transolver_unit_area']['mean']['unif']:.4f} ({V['transolver_unit_area_over_uniform_unif']:.1f}x), so GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA becomes {V['gt_unit_over_isla_area_unif']:.1f} and "
      f"Transolver ÷ ISLA {V['transolver_unit_over_isla_area_unif']:.1f}. Float32, two seeds, 180 validation wings, 200,000 cells per case; data: results/trainarea_reduction_2026-09-20.json.")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The frame price (diagnostic, legacy centered variant; pending at the reporting protocol)"}
The program's earlier configuration, the legacy centered variant (plain-mean
center, constant length unit; @sec-isla-variants), was measured on every
rung, and ISLA pays a price against it that depends on whether validation
geometries recur in training: largest at 35 and 210 cases, where every
validation geometry appears in training at other angles, and at the fixed
angle; smallest on the two never-seen-geometry rungs; nothing on
DrivAerML. The sizes are being re-measured at the reporting protocol and
are not quoted here. The price is a mesher pattern, not lost position: on
the 35-case and fixed-angle splits a diagnostic ISLA handed the exact frame
of the full geometry as global data, so lacking no positional information,
paid as much or more. What the plain-mean centroid reads is where the
mesher placed its cells, which displaces that centroid by 0.131 body
lengths on these wings and 0.034 on DrivAerML cars, a reusable cue exactly
when the same geometries recur or a single angle fixes the refinement
pattern. That content is discretization-dependent and ISLA declines to
carry it (@sec-principle); the consistency benchmark of
@sec-consistency-bench is where it earns its price.
Data: results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json,
results/udrvl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/udrvl_510_reduction_2026-09-12.json,
results/frame_reduction_2026-09-11.json.
:::

## Controls {#sec-de-controls}

**The two-seed spread at small rungs understates the uncertainty by a
factor of three to eleven; the training draw is the larger source, and the
ordering holds on every draw.** The 35-case split is one random draw from
the pool. The control re-ran GeoTransolver, Transolver and the ISLA
configuration of the time, the legacy centered variant (removed; the
interval measures the draw, not the configuration), on three further
geometry-stratified 35-case draws, three seeds each: GeoTransolver ÷ variant
lies between 0.88 and 0.96 across draws (mean 0.91, 90% interval 0.84 to
0.98) and Transolver ÷ variant between 0.85 and 0.90 (mean 0.87, interval
0.82 to 0.92); the curated draw is typical for every arm. At 210 cases the
same design gives 0.87 (0.82 to 0.93) and 0.90 (0.85 to 0.95). Every
35-case and 210-case ratio in the book is to be read with a between-draw
spread of this size; the ladder above carries seed-mean ratios of the
curated draw alone. Data:
research/transfer_program/studies/campaign_a_draws/campaign_a_n35_fp32_2026-09-10.json
and campaign_a_n210_fp32_2026-09-10.json.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The other steel-man controls"}
- **Learning rate.** GeoTransolver receives a two-rate control, 1e-3 and
  3e-3, and the better lane is reported; at the reporting protocol that is
  3e-3 on the wings (@sec-lr-protocol). Transolver at 1e-3 is worse than at
  3e-3 at 35 cases and stays at 3e-3.
- **Seeds.** Third seeds at 35 and 210 cases move neither baseline's mean by
  more than 0.001.
- **The surface measure.** Giving GeoTransolver and Transolver the same
  quadrature measure ISLA carries, in their slice pooling, costs them a few
  percent at 35 cases and leaves them ahead of ISLA; the price is being
  re-measured at the reporting protocol. These measure-weighted baselines
  are ablations that locate a property, not modifications of the
  public models.
- **ISLA's own controls** are the single-factor ablations of @sec-mechanism.

Data: results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json,
results/mw_w4dr_xfam_reduction_2026-09-10.json.
:::

## What ISLA's error responds to {#sec-de-strata}

**ISLA's error is paid for in geometries, not cases; it tracks the flow
physics case by case; and the deficit to GeoTransolver and Transolver at
the protocol width is representational.** Three observations about ISLA
alone.

*Geometry count.* Cutting the training geometries six- to eight-fold at a
similar case count (4 geometries at ten angles against 35 cases on 33
geometries; 21 geometries against 210 cases on about 126) costs ISLA 1.5 to
1.8x. The comparison changes the validation population as well as the
training composition, so it supports a geometry-count reading and not the
stronger statement that geometry count alone sets the error.

*Flow difficulty.* ISLA's error is about twice as large post-stall as in
attached flow, it interpolates smoothly at the one angle absent from
training, and its residual concentrates where the geometry is intricate:
the slat and flap gaps hold about 15% of the sampled points and most of the
squared error. The per-band table is in the collapsed note below.

*Capacity.* Trained and evaluated on one case at a time (64 sampled views of
a single wing), ISLA's one-car floor, the converged error on a single
training case, is 1.27x GeoTransolver's and 1.37x Transolver's, wider than
the 35-case gap, and the deficit sits on the smooth, large-cell open
surfaces rather than at the gaps. A deficit that widens when the data are
held fixed is not a data limit; it is representational at the protocol
width, and the DrivAerML anatomy of @sec-deficit-anatomy locates it
(results/overfit_single_case_2026-09-11.json). Representational is not
the same as architectural: on DrivAerML, given width and depth, both
architectures reach the same floor of about 0.040 (@sec-scoreboard-floor),
so on that dataset the protocol-width deficit is capacity that ISLA
recovers with depth. Whether the same holds on the wings is a
single-dataset gap the wing scaling study closes (@sec-program-status).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The per-band residual and the seen-geometry effect (diagnostic, legacy centered variant)"}
These three measurements were made on the legacy centered variant. On the
35-case split its error is 0.09 to 0.10 in attached flow (4° to 12°) and
0.17 to 0.19 post-stall, and its per-case error rises with angle of attack
(rank correlation 0.56 at 35 cases, 0.61 at 210). Seeing a geometry at
another angle helps it by 15% at 35 cases
(results/hilift_seen_vs_unseen_geometry_2026-09-07.json).

| training cases | near band (0.7–2% chord), about 15% of points | 2–10% of chord, about 6% of points | open surface (>10%), about 79% of points |
|---|---|---|---|
| 35 | 59% | 4% | 36% |
| 210 | 71% | 4% | 23% |

: Where ISLA's residual pressure error lives on the 35- and 210-case splits (legacy centered variant, two-seed mean predictions, median over the 180 validation cases): the share of ISLA's squared error in each band of distance to the nearest facing surface, with the median share of sampled points each band holds. The facing-surface distance is the local gap or cove width and is infinite on an open convex surface. Data: results/hlreg_facing_distance_35_2026-09-08.json, results/hlreg_facing_distance_210_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-hilift-hlreg}
:::

## Other readouts: forces and an uncertainty signal {#sec-de-forces}

**Two further readouts exist for ISLA alone and are pending at the
reporting protocol: the integrated lift and drag coefficients of the
validation cases, and the disagreement between two seeds as a ranking of
per-case error.** Both were measured on the removed legacy centered variant
in the exploration runs (results/hilift_paired_stats_2026-09-06.json,
results/hilift_ensemble_uq_{35,210,1260}_2026-09-06.json) and are being
re-measured on ISLA at the reporting protocol; their values are not quoted
here. The force reference is the CFD label integrated on the same sampled
cells as the prediction, so the sampling error of the integral cancels; how
far a sampled integral sits from the full-surface force is not measured.
The uncertainty readout tests ranking, not calibration. GeoTransolver's and
Transolver's forces and seed signals are not reduced, so neither is a
comparison.

## What each ingredient costs ISLA {#sec-mechanism}

**No single ingredient is load-bearing for ISLA's accuracy: the relational
invariants are the largest single ingredient, and the measure weights cost
in distribution as an estimator-variance effect that shrinks with cell
count.** The single-factor ablation that established the ordering was run
on the program's earlier configuration, the legacy centered variant, at 35
cases; its prices are being re-measured at the reporting protocol, so the
collapsed note states what was varied and the mechanism of the
measure-weight price and quotes no price.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The single-factor ablation and the price of the measure weights (diagnostic, legacy centered variant; prices pending at the reporting protocol)"}
Removing one ingredient at a time from the legacy centered variant at 35
cases, two seeds, frozen protocol, shared validation set
(results/a35_v0_reduction_2026-09-05.json), varied five things: raw
coordinates added as inputs (breaking exact equivariance); the invariant
seeds replaced by the raw vectors; the similarity gauge switched on; the
measure weights switched off (the ablation, never adopted); and the
relational invariants removed from routing and read-back. Every variant
retains an invariant path somewhere, so the ablation speaks to exactness
and to individual ingredients, not to the presence of invariant
information. Its ordering: exactness of the equivariance and the invariant
seed set are not load-bearing in distribution; the similarity gauge, a
center and length unit estimated from the sample, costs the variant a few
percent on this rung (on ISLA at 435 cars the price of not being told the
body's center is inside seed noise, @sec-nb-sgref-verdict); the weights-off
ablation gains; and removing the relational invariants is the largest
single loss. Each size is pending at the reporting protocol.

**Measure weights are a correctness requirement, and the mechanism of
their in-distribution price is known.** Turning them off improves the
legacy centered variant on every wing rung and slightly on DrivAerML (the
sizes are pending at the reporting protocol). The price has two parts. One
is estimator variance: with the weights on, the effective number of tokens
per slice is about a fifth of the count, and on DrivAerML the weights-off
advantage shrinks from 11% at 2,500 cells to 2.4% at 40,000. The other, on
the wings, is mesh-pattern content: there the advantage is flat at 12 to
13% from 2,500 to 40,000 cells, which variance cannot be, and under
area-proportional resampling it inverts, the weights-off model's error
rising above that of predicting zero while the weighted model's falls with
count (@sec-consistency-bench). A configuration that reads the mesher's
cell placement is not a surrogate for the surface (@sec-principle); the
weights-off ISLA is an ablation and never a configuration. Data:
results/nowl_210_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/geo210_all_arms_2026-09-10.json,
results/now_single12_reduction_2026-09-10.json,
results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09d.json.
:::

## The same protocol on DrivAerML {#sec-de-drivaerml}

**On DrivAerML, GeoTransolver is the more data-efficient model by a
deficit that narrows monotonically from 17% at 27 cars to zero at 435.** At
the reporting protocol of 200,000 cells, with each architecture at its own
best rate (GeoTransolver's is 3e-3 on every rung at this budget,
@sec-lr-protocol), GeoTransolver ÷ ISLA runs from 0.83 at 27 training cars
to 1.00 at 435, and Transolver ÷ ISLA stays within 0.99 and 1.06 on every
rung; the five rungs with seeds and rates are @tbl-scoreboard-200k. This is
not an ISLA advantage: it is a deficit that closes at the full training set.
The deficit is uniform in every way measured: the same on every third of
the car, a near-constant factor per car on a difficulty ordering both
architectures share (per-case rank correlation 0.86 to 0.89, equal to each
architecture's correlation with its own second seed), and the same for the
surface and the volume
(results/drivaer_percase_correlation_2026-09-07.json).


## Limits of the claim {#sec-de-limits}

- **The ladder is a data-efficiency measurement, not a scaling law.** Its
  rungs span the range of data every production CFD dataset in this program
  occupies, and the curves flatten over it. On DrivAerML the flattening has
  a measured cause: every model's error is flat in the cell count above 100,000, and
  given width and depth both architectures reach the same floor of about
  0.040 (@sec-scoreboard-floor, @sec-shared-floor). On the wings the
  corresponding scaling picture is pending (@sec-program-status), so the
  wing flattening is not yet attributed.
- **It is in-distribution and a validation-set figure.** The validation
  cases share the training design; the checkpoints are final-epoch with no
  selection, but the validation set was reused adaptively for the baselines'
  per-rung learning rate and for what to present, and the sealed test was
  spent on regime extrapolation (@sec-limits-validation). Across a regime
  boundary no architecture generalizes (@sec-regime-extrapolation).
- **Seeds do not measure the choice of training cases.** The draw intervals
  of @sec-de-controls are the uncertainty to read, and they exist only at 35
  and 210 cases.
- **No mechanism of an in-distribution ISLA accuracy advantage is
  established, because no such advantage is established.** At the reporting
  protocol ISLA reaches parity with GeoTransolver at full DrivAerML data and
  trails it below (@sec-de-drivaerml); on the wings it trails at every rung
  under the training convention. What ISLA buys is stated elsewhere, each
  with its scope: exact pose covariance, worth 12% and 21% over the
  rotation-augmented GeoTransolver and Transolver on posed DrivAerML cars
  (@sec-pose-contract); a trained function that is weakly dependent on the
  law the training sample was drawn by, 1% on these wings and 8% on the cars
  against factors of 2.4 to 9.6 for GeoTransolver and Transolver
  (@sec-de-training-law, @sec-training-law); a frame that converges under
  refinement (@sec-consistency-bench); the interior velocity lead of 42% on
  DrivAerML, single dataset (@sec-interior); and the accuracy-against-memory
  frontier on DrivAerML at the 100,000-cell scaling budget, where its best
  configuration at or under each training-memory budget is at least as
  accurate as GeoTransolver's (@sec-scoreboard-floor).
- **The wing deficit is not count noise.** On the two rungs measured at both
  budgets, twenty times the sampled cells moved the ratio by 0.01 (35 cases,
  where no model moved by more than 4%) and 0.04 (fixed angle, where every
  model improved by 20 to 25%) (@tbl-scoreboard-200k-wings); the deficit is
  a property of the trained functions, and its mechanism, the mesher pattern
  where validation geometries recur in training, is the open study
  (@sec-open-questions).
